identity_evidence.quote: We report a rare case, a novel mixed cavernous hemangioma of the body associated with a capillary hemangioma of the cervix in a patient of 28 years 5th visors with recurrent genital bleeding in the postpartum period leading to a hysterectomy
28 years old multiparous that we had received 02 hours after a vaginal delivery

attribution_limitations: The case text refers to the patient as "she" in four sentences but uses the possessive "His" once ("His medical history was featureless"), and the discussion prints "his admission". The repeated subject pronoun "she" is used for documented sex; the possessive slips are kept review_only as an ambiguity, not a conflict.

The admission platelet count is printed "23 0000 platelets" in the case text and "23,000 platelets" in the discussion; read as a print artefact of one admission blood count, with the cleaner discussion print used for the numeric value.
The abstract describes the patient as "28 years 5th visors"; the meaning of "5th visors" is unclear, while the case text and introduction say multiparous.
The sentence "she was going after an amendment to the clinical symptoms and normal laboratory tests" is unclear: it does not say that the patient was discharged, and "amendment" is not defined.
The examination finding "an absence of vaginal and perineal cervical lesions" is grammatically unclear about whether cervical, vaginal and perineal lesions are three separate sites or two.
The discussion sentence ends "in the immediate postpartum uterus and retracted with a soft tissue integrity"; the subject of "retracted" and the site of the bleeding are not explicit.
"In the absence of arterial embolization" does not say whether embolization was not indicated, not available or not performed.

"None of the above treatments had been undertaken in our patient" follows a list of conservative measures and a general statement that the tumor implies conservative treatment with regular monitoring, while the case text reports treatment based on drugs and strict regular monitoring; the scope of "the above treatments" is therefore not fully explicit.

The discussion says computed tomography angiography, magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasound-guided biopsy could help diagnosis and that the patient was financially limited and could only carry out a transvaginal Doppler ultrasound; it never states that CT angiography, MRI or biopsy were ordered or not performed.
The conclusion describes "a mixed form combining cavernous hemangioma capillary myometrium and cervix"; the wording is garbled and does not itself assign each hemangioma type to a site.
